title: Russia's war will not end until Putin accepts Ukrainian independence
gist: Peter Dickinson argues Putin's war reflects centuries of Russian imperial opposition to Ukrainian statehood, making a negotiated settlement based on mutual concessions impossible. He contends the war will only end when Putin is forced to accept an independent Ukraine, and that Western escalation-avoidance has prolonged the conflict.

insights.claim: Russia's opposition to Ukrainian statehood is one of the oldest struggles in European history, with methods ranging over centuries from bans on Ukrainian language and culture to the deliberate mass starvation of entire communities.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Framing the war as a centuries-long imperial project implies it will not be resolved by transactional diplomacy.

insights.claim: A notorious 1863 Russian imperial decree banning Ukrainian literature declared that a separate Ukrainian language never existed, does not exist, and shall not exist.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Historical precedent the author uses to argue today's identity-erasure campaign is continuity, not aberration.
insights.quote: a separate Ukrainian language never existed, does not exist, and shall not exist.

insights.claim: Putin views reconquest of Ukraine as essential to reverse the Soviet breakup and revive the Russian Empire, and fears an independent democratic Ukraine could catalyze the next phase of Russian imperial retreat.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: If Ukraine's independence is existential to Putin's project, the conflict has no negotiated off-ramp acceptable to both sides.

insights.claim: Putin has escalated his rhetoric since 2022, likening the invasion to Peter the Great's conquests and declaring in summer 2025 his belief that 'all of Ukraine is ours.'
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Explicit maximalist statements undercut assumptions that Putin would settle for territorial concessions.
insights.locator: Since the outbreak of hostilities in 2022

insights.claim: The February 2014 seizure of Crimea, followed by the Kremlin-led intervention in Donbas, set the stage for the full-scale invasion of 2022 after Putin's earlier attempts to undermine Ukraine from within failed.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: The escalation pattern suggests each unpunished step emboldened the next, a template for assessing future Russian moves.
insights.locator: During the early years of his reign

insights.claim: In Kremlin-controlled areas, all traces of Ukrainian language, culture, history, and identity are being erased, thousands have been detained in a campaign UN monitors classified as a crime against humanity, and remaining residents are forced to accept Russian passports.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: UN classification of crimes against humanity raises the legal and moral bar against any settlement legitimizing occupation.
insights.locator: The actions of the Russian army

insights.claim: Dickinson argues there can be no meaningful compromise between Russia's genocidal intentions and Ukraine's desire to survive, making all talk of a negotiated settlement futile.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: A direct challenge to market and diplomatic assumptions that a near-term ceasefire deal is achievable.
insights.quote: there can be no meaningful compromise between Russia’s genocidal intentions and Ukraine’s desire to survive.

insights.claim: Dickinson contends Western emphasis on avoiding escalation and ensuring Ukraine's survival without provoking Putin is a strategic blunder that has prolonged the war and emboldened Russia.
insights.speaker: Peter Dickinson
insights.so_what: Argues the escalation-management approach favored by many partners is counterproductive, a signal on the debate shaping Western aid policy.
insights.quote: This emphasis on avoiding escalation is a strategic blunder that has only served to prolong the war
